title: Dominic and the Bridge
premise: In 1911, Mirabel Ravensworth drives for suffragist Adeline Croft and quietly reads the letters she carries, convinced that history is made elsewhere. When a census taker's probing questions expose that Mirabel's late mother was a Ravensworth heiress erased from the family will, Mirabel discovers documents proving the inheritance was stolen through forged lunacy papers—and that Adeline's own family was complicit. Smuggling the evidence past three checkpoints to a Chancery barrister, Mirabel must choose between the movement she serves and the justice her mother never received; the book ends with the will overturned, Mirabel renouncing the fortune to fund a refuge for women like her mother, and Adeline, disgraced but changed, driving for her instead.
about_author: Tamsin Vasquez is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing Edwardian estate papers and the silences between them. She writes from a converted stable in Yorkshire, where she keeps her grandmother's 1911 census card framed above her desk.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. During the 1911 census, an unusually persistent enumerator asks about Mirabel's mother's maiden name, rattling her. She deflects, but that night she opens a letter she'd normally deliver sealed—and finds a solicitor's inquiry about a 'Mirabel Ravensworth, born 1889.' The beat: the illusion of invisibility cracking.

chapters.title: Letters I Was Never Meant to Read
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, flashback-woven. She reflects on years of reading Adeline's correspondence, justifying it as devotion. A second letter arrives from the solicitor, Halloway, hinting at 'irregularities' in a 1893 will. Emotional beat: guilt curdling into hunger for the truth about her mother.

chapters.title: The Governess Who Vanished
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She visits her old nurse, Mrs. Tallow, who reveals her mother Eleanor was a Ravensworth by birth, married beneath herself, and died in an asylum after her brothers declared her insane. Beat: grief and fury; the census question was no accident—someone has been searching for Mirabel.

chapters.title: Adeline's House of Glass
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. We see the suffragist household from above: Adeline's charisma, her debts, and her brother Gerald's visits. Gerald Ravensworth is Mirabel's uncle—Adeline married into the family that erased Mirabel's mother. Beat: dramatic irony; the reader sees what Mirabel suspects.

chapters.title: The Forged Lunacy Papers
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Posing as a cleaner, she searches Gerald's townhouse and finds the commitment order for her mother—signed with a witness's name she recognizes as Adeline's father. Beat: cold clarity; the movement's sainted family built its fortune on her mother's ruin.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Weighs
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. Adeline, sensing Mirabel's distraction, confides her fear that Gerald is diverting movement funds. She asks Mirabel to drive her to Chancery Lane—an errand that will matter later. Beat: tenderness between them, deepening the coming betrayal.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Railway Porter
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She decides to carry the stolen documents to Halloway in London, sewn into a cushion. At the station, a porter—clearly paid by someone—inspects her luggage. She talks her way through, but knows she was recognized. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Man from Halloway's Chambers
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In London, Halloway's junior clerk, Elias Finch, examines the papers and confirms the forgery is provable—but the original will register copy is held at the family's country estate, past two more checkpoints. Beat: hope with a price attached.

chapters.title: Gerald's Offer
chapters.summary: Gerald's POV. Gerald confronts Mirabel, offering money and passage to Canada if she disappears. He reveals Adeline knew of the asylum years ago and said nothing. Beat: poison in the well; Mirabel can no longer trust her own side.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Motor Car
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Driving Adeline home, Mirabel forces the truth into the open. Adeline admits she knew—and argues the movement needed Gerald's money, that some injustices must wait. Beat: the central rupture; loyalty versus justice.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Estate Gates
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, with Mrs. Tallow's help. They infiltrate a Ravensworth house party, Mirabel posing as hired staff. She reaches the estate archive but finds the will register already removed—Gerald anticipated her. Beat: despair; the enemy is always one step ahead.

chapters.title: The Second Copy
chapters.summary: Elias Finch's POV. Finch discovers the Chancery register itself holds an older enrollment of the 1893 will—different from Gerald's version. But retrieving it requires a court order, which requires a witness willing to testify publicly. Beat: the plan pivots; the evidence must be a person, not a paper.

chapters.title: The Witness in the Asylum
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She traces the nurse who witnessed her mother's commitment, now elderly and destitute, hiding in a parish workhouse. The nurse, Ruth, agrees to testify—but is frail and terrified. Beat: compassion; justice requires carrying others, not just documents.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Rectory
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Someone informs on Ruth's location. Men arrive to move her to a private asylum before she can sign an affidavit. Mirabel arrives minutes late, finding the rectory ransacked. Beat: dread; the stakes turn bodily.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Night Crossing
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel finds Ruth hidden by sympathetic workhouse women and smuggles her through a police cordon at the county line, using Adeline's motor and forged suffrage-march passes as cover. Beat: the movement's own tactics, turned to Mirabel's private justice.

chapters.title: Adeline's Choice
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. Gerald threatens to expose Adeline's knowledge of the forgery unless she denounces Mirabel publicly. Adeline, cornered, drafts the statement—then burns it. Beat: redemption earned at cost; she chooses Mirabel over the movement's funding.

chapters.title: The Affidavit
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Ruth signs the affidavit in Halloway's chambers while Gerald's solicitors besiege the building. Finch files the court order as bailiffs arrive to seize the papers. Beat: breathless climax approach; the law finally begins to move.

chapters.title: Chancery, Third Day
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In court, Gerald's counsel paints Mirabel as a thieving servant reading her betters' letters. Halloway turns it: her reading is how the truth survived at all. Beat: the theme made explicit—justice outside the law prepared the way for justice within it.

chapters.title: The Verdict and the Price
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The 1893 will is upheld; the lunacy order declared forged; Gerald ruined. Mirabel inherits—but the victory feels hollow, her mother beyond reach of any remedy. Beat: the price of survival named aloud; winning is not the same as healing.

chapters.title: What Mirabel Renounces
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She endows a refuge for women wrongly committed, in her mother's name, and declines the estate. Gerald, broken, asks why; she answers that inheritance is not what you take but what you carry forward. Beat: resolution of the inheritance theme.

chapters.title: The Driver at the Wheel
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. Adeline, publicly diminished and privately freed, takes work driving for the new refuge. She and Mirabel reach an uneasy, honest peace—no more letters read in secret, everything said aloud. Beat: reconciliation without erasure.

chapters.title: Census, 1921
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, closing frame. Ten years on, a new census taker asks Mirabel's name and occupation. She answers plainly: Ravensworth, keeper of the Eleanor Refuge. Beat: full-circle transformation—from invisibility chosen to visibility claimed.
